title: How the Warriors Have Fallen
sum: Three days after his victory over the Amalekites, David hears the news from Gilboa. A young Amalekite arrives with torn clothes, says that Saul and Jonathan are dead, and claims that he killed the wounded king at Saul's own request. He hands over Saul's crown and armlet. David and his men tear their clothes, weep and fast. Then David asks the man how he dared to destroy the LORD's anointed, and has him put to death on his own word.

The chapter ends with David's lament for Saul and Jonathan, "The Bow," from the lost Book of Jashar. It is one of the great poems of the Bible: "How the warriors have fallen!" It curses the mountains of Gilboa, praises father and son as swift and strong, calls Israel's women to weep for Saul, and mourns Jonathan's love as more wonderful than the love of women. It never mentions God, or Saul's long hunt for David.
readings: Read as history and politics

The chapter clears David of Saul's death. He was far away fighting Amalek; he punished the man who claimed to have killed Saul; and he mourned in public. Historians who read Samuel as a defense of David's rise see each step as answering the charge that David, a Philistine vassal, gained from Saul's fall.
Read as poetry and grief

The lament is not politics. It honors an enemy who tried to kill the singer, and it loves a friend whose death cost the singer most. Its refrain, its curse on the land, and its silence about God make it a song of pure human loss, the model for later laments in Israel.

views.H: The traditional reading takes both the Amalekite's lie and David's grief as real. The lament was preserved in the Book of Jashar and copied into Samuel, an authentic poem of David's.
views.C: Critical scholars generally accept the lament as old, perhaps genuinely David's. Many see the prose frame as part of the History of David's Rise, an apology answering charges that David had a hand in Saul's death. The two accounts of Saul's death (1 Samuel 31; 2 Samuel 1) are either harmonized or seen as separate traditions.
views.L: Literary readers point to the echoes: the runner with torn clothes recalls the Benjaminite who brought Eli bad news (1 Samuel 4:12); an Amalekite carries the crown of the king who lost his throne over Amalek; and the refrain "How the warriors have fallen" divides the song in three.
views.J: Jewish tradition holds the love of David and Jonathan as the model of love that does not depend on any selfish cause (Mishnah Avot 5:16). Rashi reads "the bow" as an order to train Judah in archery.
views.X: Christian readers have admired David's love for his enemy and seen in it something of the command to love enemies (Matthew 5:44).

deep.b: The song (1:19–27) has three parts marked by the refrain "How the warriors have fallen!" The first (1:19–24) is for Saul and Jonathan together: do not tell the Philistines, let Gilboa be cursed, remember their courage, weep for the king. The second (1:25–26) narrows to Jonathan alone and to David's own grief. The last line (1:27) closes with the refrain and the loss of the "weapons of war." Some hear in places the limping beat of the qinah, a long line followed by a shorter one, but most scholars find the song's rhythm freer than strict dirge meter.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the lament and the gazelle
deep.b: My own suggestion: the word tsevi that opens the lament, "splendor" or "gazelle" (1:19), is picked up in the next chapter when Asahel runs "like one of the gazelles" (2:18) and dies for it. If the narrator placed these on purpose, the gazelle becomes the image of young courage that runs to its death: Jonathan on the heights, Asahel on the road to Gibeon. Commentators have noted the double meaning of tsevi in 1:19; linking it with 2:18 as a deliberate thread is my own reading, and it rests on only two uses of the word.

echoes: 1 Samuel 31:1–13; 1 Samuel 4:12; 1 Samuel 15:1–35; 1 Samuel 24:6; 1 Samuel 26:9; 1 Samuel 18:1–4; 1 Samuel 20:41–42; Joshua 10:13; Micah 1:10; 4:10; 1 Chronicles 10:1–14

settings.by: a young Amalekite, the son of a resident foreigner
settings.to: David, at Ziklag
settings.when: three days after the battle on Mount Gilboa
settings.why: The man claims he killed Saul at Saul's own request, and he hands David the crown and armband. He expects a reward. His story does not match 1 Samuel 31:4–5, where Saul falls on his own sword, so most readers think he is lying to win favor. The scene lets readers see that the crown came to David, but not by David's hand.

settings.to: the Amalekite messenger, in front of David's men
settings.when: after the day of mourning for Saul and Jonathan
settings.why: David asks how the man dared to harm the LORD's anointed, and has him killed on the word of his own mouth. The act proves to David's men and to every reader that David took no joy in Saul's death and punished anyone who claimed to have caused it.
views: Traditional readers see a principle David held all his life, already shown in 1 Samuel 24 and 26.
Scholars such as P. Kyle McCarter see the story told to clear David of any part in Saul's death, at a time when that charge was alive.

settings.what: The song of the bow: David's lament for Saul and Jonathan
settings.to: the people of Judah, who were to learn it; it was written in the Book of Jashar
settings.when: after he hears that Saul and Jonathan are dead
settings.why: David honors Saul and Jonathan as warriors, begs that the news not reach the Philistine cities, and curses the mountains of Gilboa. He calls on Israel's women to mourn the king who dressed them in scarlet, and he grieves for Jonathan, whose love was "more than the love of women." The refrain "How the warriors have fallen!" frames it. The song was taught to Judah, David's own tribe, so that it would grieve for Saul and not rejoice. It shows David honoring the house he replaced.
views: Traditional readers, and many critical scholars too, think the lament is genuinely old and likely David's own, because of its early language and its source in the Book of Jashar.
Most readers take verse 26 as deep friendship and covenant loyalty. Some modern readers think it suggests a romantic bond. The Hebrew word for love is used for both.

title: Two Kings and a Civil War
sum: David asks the LORD where to go and is sent to Hebron, where the men of Judah anoint him king. He thanks the men of Jabesh-gilead for burying Saul, and invites them to accept him. Meanwhile Abner, Saul's commander, makes Saul's son Ish-bosheth king of the rest of Israel at Mahanaim, across the Jordan. Israel has two kings.

At the pool of Gibeon, Abner and Joab set twelve young men from each side against each other in a deadly "contest"; all twenty-four die, and a battle follows. Joab's swift brother Asahel chases Abner and will not turn aside, and Abner kills him with the butt of his spear. At sunset Abner calls for peace, "Will the sword keep eating forever?" Joab sounds the horn. But Asahel's blood will not be forgotten.
readings: Read as the rise of David

David waits, asks God, and is chosen by his own tribe. He does not attack Saul's house; Saul's men attack first. The numbers at the end (twenty dead against 360) show God's favor moving to David's side.
Read as a tragedy of brothers

The chapter is about Israel killing Israel. The duel is called a game, the soldiers are "brothers," and the young man who will not turn aside dies on the road. Abner's question, "Will the sword keep eating forever?", hangs over the rest of the book.

views.H: Traditional readers place David's anointing at Hebron about 1010 BC. The rival kingdom of Ish-bosheth east of the Jordan reflects Philistine control of the west after Gilboa.
views.C: Critical scholars note the chronological strain between Ish-bosheth's two years and David's seven and a half (2:10–11), and some suggest that Ish-bosheth's reign began years after Saul's death. Many see Abner, not Ish-bosheth, as the real power.
views.L: Literary readers notice the gazelle (2:18; compare 1:19), the play of "turn aside" (four times in 2:19–23), and the way Asahel's death sets up Abner's murder in chapter 3.
views.J: The Talmud returns to Asahel's death when it judges Joab: Abner could have stopped Asahel by wounding a limb, so his killing was not fully lawful, yet Joab's revenge was still murder (Bavli Sanhedrin 49a). Rashi and Radak explain the place name Helkath-hazzurim and the shape of the duel.
views.X: Christian readers have often drawn from Abner's plea a lesson against strife among believers, who are also "brothers."

deep.b: The two capitals show the map of a divided land. Hebron was the heart of Judah, home of Abraham's tomb and Caleb's clan. Mahanaim lay in Gilead, beyond the Jordan, where Saul's house had loyal friends like the men of Jabesh. The Philistines, victorious at Gilboa, held the Jezreel Valley between them (1 Samuel 31:7). The list in 2:9, Gilead, the Ashurites, Jezreel, Ephraim, Benjamin, may move from claims Abner actually held to claims he hoped to win. David's kingdom grows by negotiation as much as by war, until the elders of all Israel come to Hebron (5:1–3).

echoes: 1 Samuel 30:26–31; 1 Samuel 31:11–13; 1 Samuel 11:1–11; 1 Samuel 17:8–10; Judges 20:46–48; 3:27; 20:10; 1 Chronicles 2:16; 1 Chronicles 11:26

settings.what: The LORD sends David to Hebron
settings.to: the LORD; the answer comes to David
settings.when: after David's lament for Saul and Jonathan, while he is still at Ziklag
settings.why: David asks whether to go up to one of Judah's towns and which one. God says, "Go up," and names Hebron. Hebron was Judah's chief town, where Abraham was buried. The oracle makes David's move to kingship God's choice, not a grab for power, and it leads straight to his anointing there (2:4).

settings.to: the people of Jabesh-gilead, east of the Jordan
settings.when: just after the men of Judah anoint him king at Hebron
settings.why: David blesses the town for burying Saul, promises to repay their loyal love, and mentions that Judah has made him king. It is both thanks and an invitation: Saul's most loyal town is asked to accept David now. Readers see David reaching out to Saul's supporters rather than fighting them.

settings.to: Joab, from a hilltop near Gibeon
settings.when: at sunset, after Abner has killed Asahel and Joab is chasing him
settings.why: Abner asks, "Will the sword keep eating forever?" and reminds Joab that they are fighting their own brothers. Joab calls off the chase. The question hangs over the whole book, where the sword keeps eating inside Israel and inside David's family (12:10).

title: The Murder of Abner
sum: The war drags on, David's house growing stronger and Saul's weaker. Six sons are born to David in Hebron by six wives. In Saul's house, Ish-bosheth accuses Abner of taking Saul's concubine Rizpah; at this, Abner explodes and swears to hand the kingdom to David. David demands one thing first: the return of his wife Michal, Saul's daughter. Michal is taken from her husband Paltiel, who follows her weeping until Abner sends him home. Abner wins over the elders of Israel and Benjamin and comes to Hebron with twenty men. David feasts him and sends him away in peace.

Then Joab comes back from a raid. He accuses Abner of spying, calls him back without David's knowledge, and stabs him in the gate of Hebron to avenge his brother Asahel. David curses Joab's house, orders public mourning, walks behind the bier, sings a short lament, and fasts until evening. All Israel sees that the king had no part in it. But David admits that he cannot control the sons of Zeruiah.
readings: Read as David's innocence

The narrator works hard to show that David did not order Abner's death: he sent him away in peace three times, knew nothing of Joab's plan, cursed Joab, mourned in public, and "all Israel understood" (3:37). The chapter shows a king who wins power without stained hands.
Read with suspicion

Some historians, such as VanderKam and Halpern, ask why so much defense was needed. Abner's death removed the one man who could have kept power in the north. The chapter may answer rumors, like Shimei's later charge that David was a man of blood (16:7–8).

views.H: Traditional readers take the account as accurate: Joab acted alone from revenge and rivalry, and David's grief was genuine. David's deathbed charge to Solomon (1 Kings 2:5) confirms that he held Joab guilty.
views.C: Critical scholars often read chapters 2–5 as royal apology. They note the parallel defenses of David in the deaths of Saul (1), Abner (3) and Ish-bosheth (4), and wonder whether David benefited more than the text admits.
views.L: Literary readers watch the repetition of "in peace" (3:21–23), the irony of Abner's "dog's head" outburst, and Paltiel's tears in a scene where Michal herself has no voice.
views.J: The Talmud praises Paltiel, who it says never touched Michal because she was David's wife (Bavli Sanhedrin 19b). In the Talmud, Joab's defense before Solomon is that Asahel was a pursuer, and the rabbis reject it (Bavli Sanhedrin 49a); David's charge to Solomon to repay Joab comes in 1 Kings 2:5–6.
views.X: Christian commentators have used David's restraint and mourning as a picture of grief over injustice, and Joab as a warning against revenge (Romans 12:19).

deep.h: Blood vengeance and the city of refuge
deep.b: Israel's law allowed the nearest relative, the "avenger of blood," to kill a murderer, but it set up cities of refuge where someone who killed without malice was safe until judged (Numbers 35:9–28; Deuteronomy 19:1–13). Hebron was one of them (Joshua 20:7). Asahel died in battle, after two warnings, so Abner was not a murderer under the law. Joab's killing of Abner in Hebron's gate is a private revenge in the very place the law meant to stop it. The sword that killed Asahel at Gibeon now kills Abner at Hebron, and Joab will use the same stroke on Amasa (20:10).

Michal is the only woman in Samuel said to love a man (1 Samuel 18:20). She saved David's life (1 Samuel 19:11–17), was given by Saul to Palti while David was a fugitive (1 Samuel 25:44), and is now taken back by David as part of a political deal. Her husband's tears are the only feelings shown. Her own voice comes once, in chapter 6, in bitterness. Readers have seen in her one of the Bible's most tragic women.

echoes: 2:18–23; 1 Samuel 18:20–27; 1 Samuel 25:44; 1 Samuel 9:16; 16:21–22; 1 Kings 2:5–6; 1 Kings 2:22; Numbers 35:9–28; Joshua 20:7; 1 Chronicles 3:1–4

settings.what: Abner's oath to bring Israel to David
settings.to: Ish-bosheth, Saul's son and king at Mahanaim
settings.when: after Ish-bosheth accuses him of sleeping with Saul's concubine Rizpah
settings.why: Stung by the charge, Abner swears to do what the LORD swore to David and transfer the kingdom from Saul's house. Taking a dead king's concubine could be a claim to the throne, so Ish-bosheth's fear was real. Abner's words show that even Saul's general knew of God's promise to David, and that the change of kingdom came from inside Saul's own camp.

settings.what: Abner talks to the elders of Israel
settings.to: the elders of the northern tribes and the men of Benjamin
settings.when: before he goes to Hebron to make a covenant with David
settings.why: Abner reminds the elders that they had wanted David as king for a long time, and quotes a promise that the LORD would rescue Israel through David. He is persuading Saul's own tribes. Readers see the north's move to David as freely chosen, not forced.

settings.to: the LORD; the curse is spoken at Hebron, and no other hearers are named
settings.when: after Joab murders Abner at the gate to avenge his brother Asahel
settings.why: David declares himself and his kingdom innocent of Abner's blood before the LORD, and calls down lasting trouble on Joab's family. A murder like this brought bloodguilt (Numbers 35:33), and David makes sure it falls on Joab, not on the throne. The curse prepares for Joab's end in 1 Kings 2:5–6, 31–33.

settings.what: David's lament and fast for Abner
settings.to: Joab and all the people at Abner's burial in Hebron, and then his servants
settings.when: at the funeral
settings.why: David orders Joab himself to mourn, walks behind the bier, chants a short lament, and refuses to eat until sunset. He tells his servants a great man has fallen and that Zeruiah's sons are too harsh for him. The narrator says the people understood the king had no part in the killing. The scene is aimed as much at Israel's tribes as at the dead man: they must believe David did not murder the general who was bringing them to him.
views: Traditional readers take David's mourning as real sorrow for a brave man.
Scholars who read the book as royal apology note how carefully the story stresses that "all Israel" saw his innocence (3:37), which suggests the charge was once made.

title: The Murder of Ish-bosheth
sum: With Abner dead, Ish-bosheth loses heart, and Israel panics. Two of his own raiding captains, Rechab and Baanah, men of Beeroth in Benjamin, come to his house at noon, slip past the sleeping doorkeeper, kill him in his bed and cut off his head. They walk all night through the Arabah and bring the head to David at Hebron, saying that the LORD has avenged the king on Saul's house.

David answers with an oath: he executed the man who claimed to have killed Saul, and these men have killed an innocent man in his own bed. He has them killed, their hands and feet cut off and hung by the pool of Hebron, and he buries Ish-bosheth's head in Abner's tomb. A short note tells of Jonathan's son Mephibosheth, lamed at five when his nurse fled with him. No son of Saul with a real claim and a following is left.
readings: Read as the end of Saul's house

Each chapter since Saul's death has removed a pillar of his house: Saul and Jonathan, Abner, now Ish-bosheth. The heir that matters most, Jonathan's son, is a crippled boy; Saul's other descendants (21:8) have no army behind them. The kingdom falls to David without his raising a hand against the LORD's anointed or his son.
Read as a pattern of justice
David responds to the assassins exactly as he did to the Amalekite (1:14–16; 4:10). He refuses to profit from murder done in his name, and the narrator lets his own words make the point.

views.H: Traditional readers accept the account: Ish-bosheth's own officers killed him, and David punished them. The note about Mephibosheth prepares for chapter 9.
views.C: Critical historians again see apology, defending David in a death that cleared his way to the northern throne. Some connect the killers' Gibeonite town with Saul's violence against the Gibeonites (21:1–2).
views.L: Literary readers point to the Greek version of 4:6, with its drowsy doorkeeper, and to the grim parallels: the head carried by night, the hands and feet that did the deed cut off.
views.J: Jewish commentators praise David's justice. Commentators note that the men condemned themselves by their own words, like the Amalekite (1:16).
views.X: Christian readers have contrasted David's refusal to seize the kingdom by violence with Jesus' refusal of the sword (Matthew 26:52) and his kingdom that is not from this world (John 18:36).

deep.b: The verse about Jonathan's son (4:4) seems out of place, but it answers a question: with Ish-bosheth dead, was there any other heir of Saul? Jonathan's son was a boy who could not walk, lamed in the panic after Gilboa. Saul did have other descendants, two sons by Rizpah and five grandsons through a daughter (21:8), but none with Abner's army behind him. His name, like Ish-bosheth's, has bosheth ("shame") in place of baal; Chronicles calls him Merib-baal (1 Chronicles 8:34). David will remember him in chapter 9.

settings.what: David's sentence on the murderers of Ish-bosheth
settings.to: Rechab and Baanah, captains in Ish-bosheth's army, at Hebron
settings.when: when they bring him the head of Saul's son
settings.why: David reminds them that he killed the man who claimed to have killed Saul, and says killing an innocent man in his own bed is worse. He has them executed and buries Ish-bosheth's head in Abner's tomb. The speech separates David from every murder that cleared his path to the throne.

title: King of All Israel, Lord of Zion
sum: All the tribes of Israel come to Hebron. They remind David that he led Israel's army even under Saul and that the LORD named him shepherd and ruler of his people. The elders make a covenant with him before the LORD and anoint him king of all Israel. David is thirty; he will reign forty years.

David marches on Jerusalem, the Jebusite city that no tribe had taken, and captures the stronghold of Zion despite the taunt that "the blind and the lame" could keep him out. He makes it the City of David. Hiram of Tyre builds him a palace; more wives and children are born to him. Twice the Philistines come up the Valley of Rephaim, and twice David asks the LORD and wins, the second time waiting for the sound of marching in the treetops.
readings: Read as nation-building

In one chapter David unites the tribes by covenant, takes a neutral capital on the border of Judah and Benjamin, wins foreign recognition from Tyre, and breaks the Philistine threat. Jerusalem, a city with no tribal history, becomes the city of the king and soon of God.
Read as God's work

Each success is credited to God: the LORD's word made David shepherd (5:2), the LORD was with him (5:10), the LORD raised his kingdom (5:12), the LORD burst through his enemies (5:20) and went out before him (5:24). David's part is to ask and obey.

views.H: Traditional readers date the capture of Jerusalem to about 1003 BC, after seven and a half years in Hebron. Archaeology confirms a fortified Bronze Age city on the ridge above the Gihon spring, though remains from David's own time are debated.
views.C: Critical scholars note that chapter 5 groups events by theme: the Philistine wars (5:17–25) probably came before the capture of Jerusalem, since David "went down to the stronghold." Minimalist historians doubt that 10th-century Jerusalem was more than a small town; others, like Eilat Mazar, point to large structures they date to David's time.
views.L: Literary readers notice the play on "burst through" (parats) at Baal-perazim, which returns at Perez-uzzah (6:8), and the strange saying about the blind and the lame that will be answered by Mephibosheth at the king's table (9:13).
views.J: Jerusalem becomes the holy city of Judaism. A midrash cited by Rashi explains "the blind and the lame" as images of Isaac and Jacob guarding a treaty Abraham had made with the Jebusites, which David had to respect until he bought the land.
views.X: Christian readers see Zion as a picture of God's city (Hebrews 12:22) and David's capture of it as a step toward the kingdom of the Son of David. They contrast the saying about the blind and the lame with Jesus healing them in the temple (Matthew 21:14).

deep.b: Jerusalem is far older than Israel. It is named in Egyptian curse texts of the 1800s BC and in letters from its king Abdi-Heba to Pharaoh in the 1300s BC (the Amarna letters). Genesis connects it to Melchizedek, king of Salem (Genesis 14:18; Psalm 76:2). Joshua and Judges say that Judah and Benjamin could not drive out the Jebusites (Joshua 15:63; Judges 1:21). The city sat on a narrow ridge, protected by valleys on three sides, with the Gihon spring at its foot. Taking it gave David a capital that belonged to no tribe, a strong fortress, and a site that would become the center of Israel's worship.

David is anointed three times: privately by Samuel (1 Samuel 16:13), by Judah at Hebron (2:4), and by all Israel's elders at Hebron (5:3). The repetition shows the book's view of kingship: God chooses, but the people must accept. The covenant in 5:3 sets terms between king and people, as Samuel had written down the rules of the kingship for Saul (1 Samuel 10:25).

echoes: 1 Samuel 16:1–13; 1 Samuel 18:16; Genesis 14:18; Joshua 15:63; Judges 1:21; Isaiah 28:21; Psalm 78:70–72; Matthew 21:14; 1 Chronicles 11:1–9; 1 Chronicles 14:1–17

settings.by: the tribes and elders of Israel, and King David
settings.to: David, and before the LORD at Hebron
settings.when: after Ish-bosheth's death, seven and a half years into David's rule over Judah
settings.why: The tribes say David is their own flesh and bone, that he led Israel's army even under Saul, and that the LORD called him to shepherd his people. Then David makes a covenant with the elders and they anoint him. The covenant bound king and tribes to each other, before the LORD. Readers see that the north chose David of its own will. When that covenant was not honored, the north broke away again (1 Kings 12:16).

settings.what: The Jebusites' taunt and David's order
settings.by: the Jebusites of Jerusalem, then David
settings.to: David and his men, then David's men
settings.when: as David attacks the fortress of Zion
settings.why: The Jebusites boast that even the blind and the lame could keep David out. David orders his men to go up through the water shaft. The narrator adds a saying from later times that the blind and lame may not come into "the house." The passage explains how the city became the City of David, and why a saying about the temple was told. Its Hebrew is hard and its meaning is still debated.

settings.what: The LORD's answers about the Philistines
settings.to: David
settings.when: when the Philistines twice spread out in the Valley of Rephaim to attack the new king
settings.why: David asks before he fights, and God answers with a plan: once "Go up," and once "Swing around to their rear," waiting for the sound of marching in the trees. Readers see the difference from Saul, whom God would not answer. The victories also show that the Philistines, who killed Saul, were broken by David.

title: The Ark Comes to Jerusalem
sum: David sets out with thirty thousand picked men to bring the ark of God from Kiriath-jearim, where it had stayed since the Philistines returned it. They load it onto a new cart, and Israel celebrates with songs and instruments. At Nacon's threshing floor the oxen stumble; Uzzah reaches out to steady the ark, and God strikes him dead. Angry and afraid, David leaves the ark at the house of Obed-edom the Gittite.

Three months later, hearing that the ark has brought blessing to Obed-edom, David tries again. This time it is carried. David sacrifices after six steps and dances before the LORD with all his strength, wearing a linen ephod, as the ark comes up with shouts and the ram's horn. Michal, Saul's daughter, watches from a window and despises him. When David comes home to bless his house, she mocks him for exposing himself before slave girls. He answers that he danced before the LORD, who chose him over her father, and that he will humble himself even more. Michal has no child to the day of her death.
readings: Read as holiness and joy

The chapter holds together two sides of God's presence. Uzzah's death shows that God is holy and cannot be handled carelessly. Obed-edom's blessing and David's dance show that the same presence brings joy. The difference lies in how God is approached: by his way, not by the Philistines' cart.
Read as the end of Saul's line

The chapter closes not with the ark but with Michal. Saul's daughter scorns David's worship, and David reminds her that God chose him over her father. Her childlessness means that Saul's line will never share David's throne.

views.H: Traditional readers see a real procession, remembered in psalms like Psalm 24, 68 and 132. Chronicles retells it at length with Levites, singers and the explanation of Uzzah's death (1 Chronicles 13; 15–16).
views.C: Many critical scholars, following Leonhard Rost, see this chapter as the end of an older "ark narrative" begun in 1 Samuel 4–6, telling how the ark came to Jerusalem. They compare ancient accounts of kings bringing a god's statue into a new capital to legitimize their rule.
views.L: Literary readers notice the word "burst out" (5:20; 6:8), the six steps and the joyful dance against the deadly cart, and the clash of "honor" between Michal and David (6:20–22). The narrator calls Michal "Saul's daughter," not David's wife.
views.J: The rabbis taught that David erred by having the ark carried on a cart, because he had called God's laws "songs" and forgot them (Bavli Sotah 35a). David's dance is a model of joy in a commandment, and the Talmud discusses Michal at length (Bavli Sanhedrin 21a).
views.X: Christian readers have seen in David's dance a model of wholehearted worship, and in Michal a warning against despising it. Some church fathers saw the ark as a figure of Christ or of Mary, who carried God's presence (compare Luke 1:39–56, where some see echoes of this chapter).

deep.b: Several scholars have noticed that Luke's account of Mary's visit to Elizabeth seems to echo 2 Samuel 6. David arises and goes to Judah (6:2); Mary arises and goes to a town of Judah (Luke 1:39). David asks, "How can I ever have the LORD's ark come to me?" (6:9); Elizabeth asks how it can be that the mother of her Lord comes to her (Luke 1:43). The ark stays three months with Obed-edom (6:11); Mary stays about three months with Elizabeth (Luke 1:56). John leaps in the womb (Luke 1:41, 1:44) as David leaps before the ark (6:16). Catholic and Orthodox writers have long called Mary the "Ark of the Covenant"; many Protestant scholars accept the echoes but read them more cautiously. Whether Luke intended them is debated.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the breakouts frame David's first years in Jerusalem
deep.b: My own reading of chapters 5–6: the root parats, "burst out," marks two places in quick succession. At Baal-perazim the LORD bursts through David's enemies (5:20); at Perez-uzzah he bursts out against David's own procession (6:8). The same power that wins David's wars can strike David's people. I suggest the narrator set the two names side by side to teach that the LORD of Armies is not a tool of the king: David can ask him to fight, but not carry him on a cart. Commentators have noted the wordplay; reading it as a deliberate lesson about the limits of royal control over God is my own suggestion, and Isaiah 28:21 may show that later readers took the Perazim story the same way.

echoes: 1 Samuel 4:1–7:2; 1 Samuel 19:11–17; Numbers 4:15; Numbers 7:9; Exodus 25:10–22; Psalm 24:7–10; Psalm 132:6–8; Psalm 68:24–27; 1 Chronicles 13:1–14; 1 Chronicles 15:1–16:3; Luke 1:39–56

settings.to: the whole crowd of Israel, men and women, in Jerusalem
settings.when: when the ark is set in its tent and the offerings are made
settings.why: David blesses the people in the name of the LORD of Armies and gives every person bread and cakes. The king acts almost like a priest. The blessing ties the new capital, the ark and the people together under the LORD's name. Solomon will do the same at the temple (1 Kings 8:14, 55).

settings.to: Michal, Saul's daughter and David's wife, at the palace
settings.when: after he dances before the ark as it enters Jerusalem
settings.why: Michal mocks him for uncovering himself before the slave girls. David answers that he danced before the LORD, who chose him over her father, and that he will be even humbler. The quarrel is about two kinds of kingship: Saul's dignity and David's joy before God. The narrator ends by saying Michal had no child, so Saul's line would not share David's throne.

traditions.q: Is Mary the new ark of the covenant?
views: Yes. Mary carried God's presence in her womb, and the Catechism calls her the ark of the covenant, the place where the Lord's glory dwells (Catechism 2676). Many Catholic teachers point to Luke 1:39–56, where Elizabeth's question and Mary's three-month stay echo 6:9–11.
Yes. Orthodox hymns greet the Mother of God as the ark gilded by the Spirit (Akathist Hymn), and the feast of her entry into the temple pictures her as the living ark brought into the holy place.
Lutherans honor Mary as the mother of God, but teach about her only what Scripture plainly says. The ark is most often read as a picture of Christ, God's presence with his people.

The ark points to Christ, in whom God came to live among people (John 1:14; Colossians 2:9). Most Baptists judge the links between Luke 1 and this chapter too slight to build a teaching on, and do not give Mary titles beyond the mother of Jesus.

traditions.q: David danced before the LORD. What may be used in worship?
views: Only what God commands in Scripture may be part of public worship, the regulative principle (Westminster Confession 21.1). Many Reformed teachers note that David danced in a festival procession, not in the regular worship of the sanctuary.
Churches may keep rites and customs that serve good order and do not go against God's word, though they earn no grace (Augsburg Confession 15). This allows more freedom in the forms of worship.

Joyful, bodily worship, with raised hands, shouts and dancing, is a fitting response to the Spirit's presence, and David's dance is often held up as a model. Pentecostal preachers warn against Michal's scorn for such worship.
Worship follows the church's received liturgy, with chant, icons and incense rather than dance. A slow circling procession called the Dance of Isaiah is part of weddings and ordinations.

title: God Promises David a House
sum: Settled in his cedar palace, with rest from his enemies, David tells Nathan the prophet that he wants to build a house for God's ark. Nathan agrees, but that night the LORD sends a different word. God has never asked for a house; he has moved with his people in a tent. Instead, the God who took David from the sheep will make him a great name and give Israel a secure place. And the LORD will make David a house: David's offspring will build a house for God's name, and God will make his throne stand forever. "I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me." If he does wrong, God will discipline him, but he will never take away his loyal love as he did from Saul.

David goes in and sits before the LORD. "Who am I, Lord GOD?" he asks. He praises God's greatness and his choice of Israel, and asks God to do what he has promised, so that his name will be great forever and David's house will be blessed for all time.
readings: Read as the heart of the Old Testament's hope

This chapter is the root of the hope for a Messiah. Psalms and prophets return to it when the dynasty is threatened or gone (Psalm 89; Isaiah 9:7; Jeremiah 33:17; Ezekiel 34:23–24; Amos 9:11). Jews pray for the coming of David's descendant; Christians proclaim Jesus as the son of David whose reign has no end (Luke 1:32–33).
Read in its own setting

Here the promise concerns David's next son, who will build the temple, and the dynasty after him. Solomon himself quotes it at the temple's dedication (1 Kings 8:15–20). Its "forever" is the ordinary language of royal grants. The later hope grew out of this, but the first readers heard a promise to a real family of kings.

views.H: Traditional readers see Nathan's oracle as a real prophecy given to David about 1000 BC, recorded by prophets of his court (1 Chronicles 29:29), and fulfilled first in Solomon and finally in the Messiah.
views.C: Critical scholars debate the oracle's layers: an early core promising David a dynasty, perhaps from Solomon's court; a temple layer (7:13); and Deuteronomistic editing in the exile. Some compare ancient Near Eastern royal grants (Weinfeld), and Siegfried Herrmann compared the Egyptian "royal novella," a story form in which a king plans a temple and receives a divine answer.
views.L: Literary readers point to the play on "house" (palace, temple, dynasty), to the reversal of who builds for whom, and to David's prayer with its seven uses of "Lord GOD" and ten of "your servant."
views.J: Jewish tradition reads the chapter as the foundation of the royal line from which the Messiah will come. The daily Amidah prays for the "sprout of David," and Psalm 89 is read as holding God to his word. Some rabbis connected 7:14's discipline with the exile of the kings.
views.X: The New Testament applies the chapter to Jesus: the angel promises him David's throne (Luke 1:32–33), Peter and Paul preach him as David's offspring (Acts 2:30; Acts 13:22–23; Romans 1:3), and Hebrews quotes 7:14 (Hebrews 1:5). Christians also see the church as the house God builds (Hebrews 3:6).

deep.b: The word "covenant" does not appear in 2 Samuel 7. Yet David later calls it "an everlasting covenant" (23:5), and in Psalm 89:3 God says he has cut a covenant for his chosen one. Psalm 132:11–12 calls it an oath. Scholars debate whether it was conditional or unconditional. Chapter 7 says that disobedience will bring discipline but not the loss of God's loyal love (7:14–15). Other passages make the throne depend on obedience (1 Kings 2:4; 1 Kings 9:4–7; Psalm 132:12). Many resolve the tension this way: individual kings could lose blessings and even the throne, but God would not abandon the line. When Babylon ended the kingdom in 586 BC, Psalm 89 turned the promise into a protest, and the prophets turned it into hope.

deep.h: From Nathan to the New Testament
deep.b: The Dead Sea scrolls show how the promise was being read before Jesus. The Florilegium (4Q174) quotes 7:10–14 and says the son is "the Branch of David" who will arise in the last days. Psalms of Solomon 17 (first century BC) prays for a son of David to rule Israel. When the New Testament calls Jesus "Son of David," it speaks into that hope. Hebrews 1:5 quotes 7:14 with Psalm 2:7, and Paul adapts 7:14 for the whole church (2 Corinthians 6:18).

echoes: Deuteronomy 12:10–11; 1 Samuel 2:35; 1 Samuel 25:28; 23:5; 1 Kings 5:3–5; 1 Kings 8:15–20; 1 Chronicles 17:1–27; 1 Chronicles 22:6–10; Psalm 2:7; Psalm 89:3–4; Psalm 89:19–37; Psalm 132:11–12; Isaiah 9:6–7; Isaiah 55:3; Jeremiah 33:17–21; Ezekiel 34:23–24; Amos 9:11; Luke 1:32–33; Acts 2:30; Acts 13:22–23; Romans 1:3; Hebrews 1:5

settings.what: Nathan's oracle: God will build David a house
settings.by: the LORD, through Nathan the prophet
settings.to: King David, in Jerusalem
settings.when: when David has rest from his enemies and wants to build a house for the ark
settings.why: God turns David's offer around. David will not build God a house (a temple). God will build David a house (a dynasty). His son will build the temple, God will be his father, and God's loyal love will never leave him as it left Saul. If the son sins, he will be punished, not rejected. David's house and throne will last forever. This promise became the foundation of Israel's hope for a king from David's line, and later of the hope for a Messiah. Exiles with no king held on to it (Psalm 89:3–4, 38–51), and the New Testament reads it as fulfilled in Jesus (Luke 1:32–33; Hebrews 1:5).
views: Traditional Jewish and Christian readers take the oracle as God's word to David, fulfilled first in Solomon and finally in the Messiah.
An old dynastic oracle, edited later

Many critical scholars think a short early promise to David's dynasty was expanded by the Deuteronomistic historian, who added the line about building a house for God's name. For readers under Josiah it backed the king; for exiles it raised the question whether a promise that says "forever" could fail.

Scholars note that here the promise has no conditions. Other passages (1 Kings 2:4; 1 Kings 9:4–7; Psalm 132:12) make it depend on whether David's sons keep God's covenant. How the two fit is a key question for readers after the fall of Jerusalem.

settings.to: the LORD, as David sits before him in the tent of the ark
settings.when: right after Nathan brings the promise
settings.why: David asks, "Lord GOD, who am I?" He praises God as the only God and Israel as the only people God redeemed for himself. Then he asks God to do what he has said, so that David's house will be blessed forever. The prayer models the right answer to God's promise: humble wonder, then trust. Readers who prayed it later were asking God to keep his word to David's line.

traditions.q: Does Jesus sit on David's throne now, or only in a future kingdom on earth?
views: The promise of an everlasting throne will be fulfilled literally when Christ returns and reigns from Jerusalem over a restored Israel for a thousand years (John Walvoord; J. Dwight Pentecost). Classic dispensationalists hold that Christ now sits on his Father's throne, not yet on David's, while progressive dispensationalists such as Darrell Bock teach that his reign on David's throne has already begun.

Jesus already sits on David's throne: his rising and his ascension to God's right hand fulfill this promise (Acts 2:30–36). His kingdom is present now and will be seen in full when he returns (Westminster Confession 8.1).

Christ's being seated at the Father's right hand began the Messiah's kingdom, which is already present in mystery in the Church (Catechism 664, 669). The Church rejects any hope of an earthly messianic kingdom within history, which it calls millenarianism (Catechism 676).

Christ reigns now, and his kingdom will have no end, as the Nicene Creed says; the Divine Liturgy begins by blessing that kingdom. The Orthodox Church does not teach a future earthly reign of a thousand years.

title: David's Wars and David's Court
sum: A summary of David's victories in every direction. He subdues the Philistines to the west and Moab to the east, killing two of every three Moabite prisoners. In the north he defeats Hadadezer of Zobah and the Arameans of Damascus, takes gold shields and great amounts of bronze, and receives gifts from the king of Hamath. In the south he strikes Edom in the Valley of Salt and sets garrisons there. Twice the narrator says, "Everywhere David went, the LORD made him win." David dedicates the plunder to the LORD.

The chapter ends with David's government: he rules all Israel with justice and righteousness, with Joab over the army, a recorder and a scribe, the priests Zadok and Ahimelech, Benaiah over the foreign guard, and David's own sons as priests.
readings: Read as the promise kept
Right after God's promise of rest and a great name (7:9–11), David's enemies fall on every side and he "makes a name." The borders reach toward the Euphrates, as promised to Abraham (Genesis 15:18).
Read as a royal record

The chapter reads like a king's inscription: victories, tribute and officials, with no story or dialogue. Its harsh treatment of Moab and its summary style make it different from the chapters around it.

views.H: Traditional readers accept the list as a summary of David's wars over many years, grouped by region, with numbers that sometimes suffered in copying (compare 1 Chronicles 18).
views.C: Critical scholars debate the size of David's "empire." Some think the list exaggerates a local chieftain's raids; others defend a significant 10th-century kingdom. Many think chapters 8 and 10 describe the same Aramean wars.
views.L: Literary readers note the refrain (8:6, 8:14), the dedication of the plunder (8:11), and the ideal of justice and righteousness (8:15) placed just before the Bathsheba story, where David will break it.
views.J: The Talmud reads 8:15 as the model of a judge who joins strict justice with charity, paying the loser's loss from his own pocket (Bavli Sanhedrin 6b). A midrash explains the harsh treatment of Moab as revenge for Moab's killing of David's family (Numbers Rabbah 14:1).
views.X: Christian readers have seen in David's reign of justice a picture of the Messiah's kingdom (Isaiah 9:7; Jeremiah 23:5), and in the nations' tribute a hint of the nations coming to Christ (Psalm 72:10–11).

deep.h: Samuel and Chronicles side by side
deep.b: 1 Chronicles 18 retells this chapter almost word for word, and comparing them helps with the text. Chronicles has "Edom" where the Hebrew of Samuel has "Aram" (8:12–13); it gives chariots in 8:4; it adds that Solomon used the bronze for the temple (1 Chronicles 18:8); it credits Abishai with the Edomite victory (1 Chronicles 18:12); and it calls David's sons "first in rank beside the king" instead of priests (1 Chronicles 18:17). Some differences are copying errors; others show the Chronicler's own concerns for the temple and the priesthood.

echoes: Genesis 15:18; Numbers 24:17; Deuteronomy 17:16; Joshua 11:6–9; 1 Kings 4:1–6; 1 Kings 11:14–25; Psalm 60:0; Psalm 72:1–11; 20:23–26; 1 Chronicles 18:1–17

title: A Place at the King's Table
sum: David asks whether anyone is left of Saul's house to whom he can show loyal love for Jonathan's sake. Ziba, a servant of Saul's household, tells him of Jonathan's son Mephibosheth, lame in both feet, living in Lo-debar east of the Jordan. David has him brought. Mephibosheth falls on his face, afraid. "Don't be afraid," David says. He restores all Saul's land to him and gives him a place at the royal table for life.

Ziba and his fifteen sons and twenty servants are to farm the land for Mephibosheth. So Mephibosheth, with his little son Mica, lives in Jerusalem and eats at the king's table like one of the king's sons.
readings: Read as loyal love

David keeps his oath to Jonathan (1 Samuel 20:14–17, 20:42). Kings usually wiped out the family of the house they replaced; David seats its heir at his own table. The word hesed runs through the chapter (9:1, 9:3, 9:7).
Read as wise politics

The last grandson of Saul now lives in Jerusalem, under the king's eye, while his land is worked by a steward loyal to David. Kindness and caution go together. The later story of Ziba's accusation (16:1–4; 19:24–30) shows how fragile the arrangement was.

views.H: Traditional readers take the chapter as a true account of David's faithfulness. Mephibosheth was five at Saul's death (4:4) and now has a son, so some years have passed since David took Jerusalem.
views.C: Many critical scholars see chapter 9 as the start of the "Succession Narrative" (chapters 9–20 and 1 Kings 1–2), which asks who will succeed David. Mephibosheth's presence at court keeps the question of Saul's house alive.
views.L: Literary readers note how the chapter answers 5:8: the lame man is brought into the king's house. Mephibosheth's lameness opens and closes the chapter (9:3, 9:13).
views.J: Jewish tradition praises David's loyalty to Jonathan as a model of keeping one's word. The Talmud also discusses David's later belief in Ziba's slander (Bavli Shabbat 56a–b).
views.X: Christian preachers often read the chapter as a picture of grace: the king seeks out a helpless enemy's heir, calls him by name, removes his fear, and seats him at his table for the sake of another (compare Luke 14:21; Ephesians 2:4–7).

deep.title: Claude's theory: three tables in 2 Samuel
deep.b: My own observation: Mephibosheth's place "at the king's table" (9:7, 9:10, 9:11, 9:13) is the first of several tables in the book. The next is the meal David gives Uriah to make him drunk (11:13), and later Barzillai is offered a place at the king's table and declines it (19:33–38), as David on his deathbed asks Solomon to let Barzillai's sons eat at his table (1 Kings 2:7). I suggest the narrator uses the king's table as a measure of David: here an act of loyal love, in chapter 11 a tool of deceit. Commentators have discussed each meal; reading them as a deliberate series is my own idea, resting on these few passages.

settings.to: Mephibosheth, Jonathan's lame son, and then Ziba, the steward of Saul's estate
settings.when: when David asks whether anyone of Saul's house is left to show loyal love to
settings.why: David gives back all Saul's land to Jonathan's son and orders Ziba and his sons to farm it, while Mephibosheth eats at the king's table. The decree keeps David's oath to Jonathan (1 Samuel 20:14–15). It is also an act of power: the last heir of Saul now lives in Jerusalem under the king's eye. Readers can see both kindness and caution in it.

title: Insult and War with Ammon
sum: When Nahash king of Ammon dies, David sends envoys to comfort his son Hanun, wanting to repay the loyal love Nahash had shown him. Hanun's officials convince him that the envoys are spies. Hanun shaves off half of each man's beard and cuts their robes at the buttocks, and sends them home in disgrace. David tells them to wait at Jericho until their beards grow back.

Knowing they have made themselves hateful to David, the Ammonites hire Aramean armies from Beth-rehob, Zobah, Maacah and Tob. Joab finds himself caught between the Ammonites at the city gate and the Arameans in the field. He splits his forces with his brother Abishai: "Be strong... The LORD will do whatever he sees is good." The Arameans flee, and the Ammonites retreat into their city. When Hadadezer brings Arameans from beyond the Euphrates, David himself crosses the Jordan and defeats them at Helam. Aram makes peace and will not help Ammon again.
readings: Read as the setting for chapter 11

This war leads straight into the Bathsheba story. In the spring Joab besieges Rabbah, the Ammonite capital, while David stays in Jerusalem (11:1). Kindness refused leads to war, and the war becomes the setting for David's fall.
Read as a story of honor and shame

Beards, robes and envoys were matters of a king's honor. Hanun's insult was a calculated act of defiance. David's care for his shamed men, letting them wait out of sight, shows a king protecting his servants' dignity.

views.H: Traditional readers see a real war about 990 BC, part of the same campaigns summarized in 8:3–8. Ammon's capital Rabbah lies under modern Amman.
views.C: Critical scholars often see chapters 10–12 as one unit, with the Ammonite war as the frame for the Bathsheba story, and debate how chapters 8 and 10 relate.
views.L: Literary readers note the word hesed (10:2) linking this chapter to the kindness of chapter 9, and the contrast between David, who offers kindness, and Hanun, who reads it as a trick.
views.J: Jewish readers weigh David's embassy against Deuteronomy 23:6, which tells Israel never to seek Ammon's welfare, and note that the text itself praises David's intention and blames Hanun's advisers.
views.X: Christian readers have used Joab's words in 10:12 as a model of courage joined with trust in God, and the shaming of the envoys as a picture of how God's messengers are often received (Matthew 21:33–39).

deep.h: Was David right to befriend Ammon?
deep.b: Deuteronomy 23:3–6 says that no Ammonite may enter the assembly of the LORD and that Israel must never seek their peace or their good. Readers have asked whether David broke this law by sending comfort to Hanun, and whether the insult and war were the result. Others answer that the law concerns admission to the assembly, not ordinary diplomacy, and that David was repaying a personal kindness. The text itself praises David's intention and blames Hanun's advisers.

settings.what: David's condolence and the Ammonite princes' suspicion
settings.to: his servants, then their new king Hanun
settings.when: when Hanun son of Nahash becomes king of Ammon
settings.why: David sends envoys to keep loyal love with Hanun, as Nahash had with him. The princes tell Hanun the envoys are spies. Their suspicion leads to the envoys' shaming and to the war in which David will meet Bathsheba (11:1). A kind act turned to insult starts the whole chain.

settings.to: his brother Abishai and the troops, before the gate of the Ammonite city
settings.when: when the Ammonites and their hired Aramean armies trap Israel between two fronts
settings.why: Joab splits the army and promises that each brother will help the other. He tells them to be strong for the people and the cities of their God, and to leave the outcome to the LORD. The charge shows the faith of David's army, and it sets the scene for chapter 11, when David stays home from this war.
